\section[punir]{punir — to punish}

\label{lesson:PT-C388-punir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the defence, then the Portuguese for the court sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: punir}
\textbf{punir} — \textquotedblleft{}to punish\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A lei pune quem conduz depois de beber.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The law punishes people who drive after drinking.}
\end{quote}

Formal; \emph{ser punido} — to be punished.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{punir} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{pūnīre} \textquotedblleft{}to punish\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{poena} \textquotedblleft{}penalty, punishment\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{punir}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{punir}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{punir}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the defence, then the Portuguese for the court sentence, then say \emph{punir} again
\end{itemize}

\section[a pena]{a pena — the penalty, the sentence served; the pity; the feather}

\label{lesson:PT-C388-pena}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the court sentence, then the Portuguese for to punish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a pena}
\textbf{a pena} — \textquotedblleft{}the penalty, the sentence served; the pity; the feather\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele cumpriu uma pena de dois anos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He served a two-year sentence.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Que pena!} — what a pity; \emph{vale a pena} — it is worth it. \emph{Uma pena} is also a feather.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pena} \textquotedblleft{}penalty, pity\textquotedblright{} is inherited from Latin \emph{poena} \textquotedblleft{}penalty, punishment\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), from Greek \emph{poin\'{\={e}}} \textquotedblleft{}blood money, fine\textquotedblright{}; \emph{pena} \textquotedblleft{}feather\textquotedblright{} is a separate word, from Latin \emph{penna}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a pena}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a pena}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the court sentence, then the Portuguese for to punish, then say \emph{a pena} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[a prisão]{a prisão — the prison; the arrest}

\label{lesson:PT-C388-prisao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to punish, then the Portuguese for the penalty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a prisão}
\textbf{a prisão} — \textquotedblleft{}the prison; the arrest\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele passou cinco anos na prisão.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He spent five years in prison.}
\end{quote}

Also the arrest: \emph{ordem de prisão} — arrest warrant.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{prisão} was borrowed from French \emph{prison} (EtymDB), which goes back to Latin \emph{prehēnsiō} \textquotedblleft{}a seizing\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), on \emph{prehendere} \textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a condenação]{a condenação — the conviction; the condemnation}

Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the penalty, then the Portuguese for the prison.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a condenação}
\textbf{a condenação} — \textquotedblleft{}the conviction; the condemnation\textquotedblright{}.

\end{quote}

\emph{Condenar} — to convict, to condemn.

\end{cousinweb}

\section[o castigo]{o castigo — the punishment}

\label{lesson:PT-C388-castigo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the prison, then the Portuguese for the conviction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o castigo}
\textbf{o castigo} — \textquotedblleft{}the punishment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O castigo foi ficar sem telemóvel uma semana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The punishment was a week without a mobile phone.}
\end{quote}

For children: \emph{ficar de castigo} — to be grounded.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{castigo} is built on \emph{castigar} \textquotedblleft{}to punish\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), inherited from Latin \emph{castīgāre} \textquotedblleft{}to correct, to punish\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{castus} \textquotedblleft{}pure\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
